newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan says lifts curbs on Bhutto's movements.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan says lifts curbs on Bhutto's movements.

text.p: Pakistan's new caretaker government said on Wednesday that it had lifted all restrictions on ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto's movements but her husband Asif Ali Zardari was still in protective custody.

Information Minister Irshad Haqqani told a news conference that Bhutto, who was confined by police to her official residence after being sacked on Tuesday, "was free to carry out political activities and go wherever she likes".
Haqqani said: "In the first 24 hours, certain restrictions were thought proper, but now she is absolutely free."
He said Bhutto would be authorised to stay in the prime minister's official house for 10 days, but not be allowed to use the residence for party meetings or protests.
"These restrictions apply only to the Prime Minister's house," Haqqani said.
He said Zardari was still in protective custody but did not say for how long, where or precisely why.
"Asif Zardari is in protective custody. It means there is something against him, some inquiry may be on, or something else may be considered," Haqqani said.
"I am not in a position to say what will happen next in Zardari's case," he added.
Zardari was taken into custody by army officers on Tuesday in the Punjab provincial capital Lahore and later flown to Rawalpindi, near Islamabad.
Investment minister in Bhutto's government, Zardari is at the centre of corruption allegations levelled against Bhutto's government. He has in the past denied any wrongdoing.
On Tuesday, Bhutto's defence minister, Aftab Shaaban Meerani, had filed a legal complaint claiming the ousted prime minister had been held "unlawfully incommunicado".
Lawyers for the caretaker government told a court on Wednesday that Bhutto was not under arrest, saying she was under police protection for her personal safety.
